extracted.intended_audience: military legal officers, War Department officials, commanders deciding reenlistment/benefits/discipline questions
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and discretionary rules for determining whether a soldier's prior service was 'honest and faithful' (affecting reenlistment, extra pay, furloughs, and character of discharge), plus related rules on enrollment, draft substitutes, desertion, and extradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination whether service was 'honest and faithful'
rubrics_metrics.description: It is within the discretion of the Secretary of War to decide whether a soldier's service during his last preceding term of enlistment was 'honest and faithful'; each case should be decided on its own merits and it is not practicable to prescribe in advance what misconduct will constitute failure to render honest and faithful service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited repeatedly (e.g., C.2158 Mar. 1896). The decision is entrusted to the Secretary; restrictions relating to deserters under other statutes do not automatically apply to the 1894 act. Examples show Secretary may authorize reenlistment even after conviction or discharge in some circumstances; but each case depends on its facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Presidential pardon on character of service
rubrics_metrics.description: A Presidential pardon restores a criminal to legal rights and relieves him of disabilities attaching to conviction, but it does not destroy the existing fact that his service was not 'honest and faithful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 22 Op. Atty. Gen., 36: pardon does not erase the factual record that service was not honest and faithful and thus does not by itself make one eligible for reenlistment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discharge as prima facie evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A dishonorable discharge is prima facie evidence that the prior service was not honest and faithful, but this is rebuttable and the Secretary of War has discretion to determine otherwise for reenlistment purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many cases cited (e.g., C.4667 July 26, 1898 and numerous later citations). The Secretary may, in view of all circumstances, waive the objection for enlistment even when discharge was dishonorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remission of unexecuted portion of sentence does not automatically restore eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Remission of the unexecuted part of a sentence (or remission of punishment) does not by itself render a soldier eligible for reenlistment if his last term of service was not honest and faithful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: soldier sentenced to dishonorable discharge with unexecuted portion remitted still held ineligible where last term was not honest and faithful (C.2769 Nov. 28, 1896; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conviction without dishonorable discharge is not conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: A conviction (e.g., for desertion) that does not include a sentence of dishonorable discharge does not conclusively render the soldier's service 'not honest and faithful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (C. W04 Jan. 1896; 2121 Mar. 1896; 3530 Sept. 1897; 3794 Jan. 1898) hold desertion without dishonorable discharge is not necessarily conclusive against honest and faithful characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board findings are advisory; Secretary's authority is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings of boards of officers (or other boards) as to whether service was honest and faithful are advisory; the Secretary of War is the authority vested with power to determine the fact and may reconsider and authorize reenlistment despite a board's adverse finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., board decision that service was not honest and faithful for furlough/retained pay purposes was advisory and Secretary could permit reenlistment (C.1197 Apr. & June 1895; 2731 Nov. 7, 1896).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desertion may be excused by subsequent honest service (case-by-case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a soldier deserted but was restored to duty (with time made good) and subsequently served honestly and faithfully through the end of enlistment, the Secretary may decide the last term was honest and faithful and authorize discharge with favorable remarks or reenlistment; such cases are judged on merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include deserter restored without trial and later discharged as sergeant with excellent character; Secretary may decide last term honest and faithful (C.2004 Jan. 22, 1896; 2121 Mar. 11, 1896; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Very strong showing required to excuse a prior desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: While the Secretary may, on the facts, determine that prior service including a desertion was nevertheless honest and faithful, it would have to be a very strong case to justify such a determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited directly (C.20991 Jan. 2, 1907) — establishes heightened burden where desertion is involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offenses normally calling for dishonorable discharge typically bar finding of honest and faithful service
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the applicant was guilty of an offense (e.g., embezzlement) that ordinarily calls for dishonorable discharge, the Secretary cannot properly determine prior services to have been honest and faithful for reenlistment purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.12741 June 30, 1902 and related citations hold such conduct generally prevents the Secretary from finding services honest and faithful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation combined with subsequent honest service can remove reenlistment objection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the dishonorable-discharge portion of a sentence is mitigated and the soldier's service continues honest and faithful to the date of discharge, he may be discharged with the remark 'service honest and faithful' and 'no objection known to his reenlistment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases C.10620 Mar. 9, 1903; C.21536 May 17, 1907 illustrate mitigation and continued good conduct leading to favorable discharge notation and reenlistment eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-martial conviction does not automatically forever stamp service as not honest and faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial and conviction by court-martial do not necessarily, as a matter of law, permanently prevent service being regarded as honest and faithful; punishment is meant to meet the offense and not to create a perpetual black mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., officer convicted by illegally constituted court — sentence null and void — was entitled to have service considered honest and faithful (C.16801 Sept. 7, 1904). General principle that conviction alone doesn't automatically preclude honest-and-faithful characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for extra pay (Spanish War acts) depends on manner and character of service
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the acts granting extra pay for service outside the United States (Jan. 12, 1899; Mar. 3, 1899), eligibility depends on the manner of serving and character of services, irrespective of enlistment circumstances or prior physical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A board's approved finding should be conclusive; if no board, the commanding officer's decision is conclusive because discretion vested in them by Secretary of War (C.6409 May 29, 1899; 15928 Mar. 10, 1904; 16801 Sept. 7, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrollment vs. muster-in: when drafted men enter service
rubrics_metrics.description: Enrollment of drafted men establishes liability to be called, but they are not in military service until accepted by the enrollment board after physical examination; no formal muster-in is necessary to effect entry into service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that acceptance by board after surgeon's physical exam put drafted man in service (P.50, 311 Nov. 23, 1891; multiple circuit citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafted man failing to report without substitute is deemed a deserter
rubrics_metrics.description: A drafted man who fails to report at the rendezvous without furnishing an acceptable substitute or paying commutation is to be deemed a deserter; the provision's object is to enforce appearance of notified men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited in relation to the enrollment act (P.50, 314 Nov. 23, 1891; C.2041 May 28, 1896; 2042 May 28, 1896).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitutes treated as if originally drawn
rubrics_metrics.description: If a name not drawn is substituted on the list of those drawn for a name that was drawn, the substituted name and person are treated as if that name had been drawn originally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.1570 July 25, 1895: substituted persons stand on same footing as drafted men for purposes of service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extradition of soldiers requires offense within demanding state's jurisdiction and proper channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Fugitives are not surrendered under extradition treaties except for offenses committed within the jurisdiction of the demanding government; requisitions must be made through diplomatic agents or proper civil authorities, or military when civil authority suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U.S. soldier in Canada who forged a check could not be extradited for an offense committed outside U.S. jurisdiction (P.53, 146 May 1892). Treaty with Mexico requires requisitions through proper authorities; unauthorized requisitions may be refused (R.38, 118 July 1876; B.29 June 1869).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest/delivery during military occupation is not international extradition
rubrics_metrics.description: During U.S. military occupation of places (e.g., Philippines, Cuba) the arrest and delivery of a soldier to U.S. civil authorities is not treated as international extradition; the War Department may direct surrender to a civil officer supplied with proper papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C.6900, 6055 Mar. 1899; 8825 June 15, 1900; 13289 Nov. 12, 1902 — War Department may lawfully direct surrender in such circumstances.
